title: Oscars: Egypt Selects Abu Bakr Shawky’s ‘The Stories’ for International Feature Race
description: Abu Bakr Shawky’s drama “The Stories” — which is inspired by how the director’s Egyptian father and Austrian mother began their love affair as pen p
body:
Abu Bakr Shawky’s drama “The Stories” — which is inspired by how the director’s Egyptian father and Austrian mother began their love affair as pen pals — has been selected as Egypt‘s entry for the Academy Award for best international feature film.

	When Shawky’s father Ahmed was an aspiring pianist in Cairo in 1967, he became pen-pals with a young Austrian woman named Liz, who is Shawky’s mother. The film spans from the late ’60s to the ’80s, and depicts life in his native country during that period from the cross-cultural prism that has formed his vision as an artist.
	

	Shawky made an international splash with his first feature, “Yomeddine,” which had the rare distinction of making the competition cut for Cannes in 2018. He followed up with Saudi-set travel movie “Hajjan,” which premiered at Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Film Festival in 2023.


	“The Stories,” which is written and directed by Shawky, is toplined by British-Egyptian actor Amir El-Masry (“The Crown”), Austria’s Valerie Pachner (“Fantastic Beasts: The Secrets of Dumbledore”) and Egyptian star Nelly Karim (“Voy! Voy! Voy!”). The film is produced by Julie Viez, Mohamed Hefzy, Alexander Glehr, Johanna Scherz, Shahinaz El Akkad and Ahmed Badawy. The production companies involved are Cinenovo, Film Clinic, Lagoonie Film Production, Film Square, Shofha Productions, Film AG, Fox in the Snow and Wrong Men.

	“The Stories” world premiered at the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival in 2025, went on to win the Golden Tanit for best film at the Carthage Film Festival in Tunisia and also played at the Red Sea fest last December.
	

	The shortlist for the 2027 Oscar nominations will be announced by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences on Dec. 15, with the final selection revealed on Jan. 21. The 99th Academy Awards ceremony is scheduled to take place on March 14 in Los Angeles.

schema.headline: Oscars: Egypt Selects Abu Bakr Shawky’s ‘The Stories’ for International Feature Race

title: Apple Reveals Apple Music Hall, a New Live Venue in London
description:
Apple is bringing a new live music venue to London.

	Located in Battersea Power Station, Apple Music Hall is a state-of-the-art venue “designed to
body:
Apple is bringing a new live music venue to London.

	Located in Battersea Power Station, Apple Music Hall is a state-of-the-art venue “designed to connect artists and fans through bespoke, intimate performances unlike anywhere else,” Apple said in its announcement on Tuesday.

	“Apple’s deep love for music dates all the way back to the very beginning, from the launch of the iPod to the long-running iTunes Music Festival to the debut of Apple Music,” Oliver Schusser, Apple’s vice president of Apple Music and international content, said in a statement. “Today, with the opening of Apple Music Hall, we are once again taking an unprecedented step further in our commitment to artists and fans by supporting live music in ways only Apple can do.”
	

	The 600-capacity venue promises that every seat “feels close to the performer” while offering the infrastructure fit for an arena tour, with a 38-foot-wide stage that can be reconfigured for in-the-round performances and a 48-speaker spatial sound system.


	Apple Music Hall is also an operational production facility, with two recording and mixing studios built to professional standards. The venue is hardwired for 16+ cameras with a broadcast control room that also supports iPhone video capture. 

	“In short, an artist can perform an intimate live show for fans at Apple Music Hall and walk out with a finished Spatial Audio recording, a broadcast-ready mix, and multicamera video — all from a single show,” a press release states. “Performances out of Apple Music Hall will also be livestreamed globally so fans outside of London can tune in to enjoy these one-time-only shows from their favorite artists.”
	

	“At Apple Music, we care deeply about music, the artists who make it and their life stories,” added Zane Lowe, Apple Music’s global creative director and lead anchor for Apple Music 1. “We’re always looking for new opportunities to connect the artists and the fans because we are fans. What better way to celebrate this relationship than a new music venue where we get to experience amazing music in an amazing space and share it with the world. Great music and memories will be made at Apple Music Hall.”

	Apple Music Hall officially opens Sept. 28. For more information on the venue and upcoming shows, check out its website.

schema.headline: Apple Reveals Apple Music Hall, a New Live Venue in London

title: Juliet Stevenson, Olivia Williams Join Tim Crouch’s ‘An Oak Tree’ at the Other Palace (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Francesca Moody Productions has unveiled further casting for Tim Crouch’s “An Oak Tree,” adding Juliet Stevenson, Olivia Williams, Sean Gilder, Bria
body:
Francesca Moody Productions has unveiled further casting for Tim Crouch’s “An Oak Tree,” adding Juliet Stevenson, Olivia Williams, Sean Gilder, Brian Gleeson, Sophie Melville, Rhashan Stone and Ria Zmitrowicz to the roster of guest artists appearing opposite Crouch during the show’s run at The Other Palace from Oct. 7-Nov. 15.

	“An Oak Tree” hinges on one rule: a fresh guest artist steps in alongside Crouch at every performance, with no prior look at the script and no rehearsal. First staged in 2005, the play has now been performed in upward of 19 countries, drawing on a pool of guest artists that has grown past 350 names, among them Frances McDormand, Geoffrey Rush, Peter Dinklage, Mike Myers, David Tennant and Phoebe Waller-Bridge.
	

	The newly confirmed dates are Olivia Williams on Oct. 10, Rhashan Stone on Oct. 11, Juliet Stevenson on Oct. 18, Sophie Melville on Oct. 25, Sean Gilder on Oct. 27, Brian Gleeson on Oct. 30 and Ria Zmitrowicz on Nov. 8.


	They join a previously announced group performing over October and November that includes Rosalie Craig, Clare Perkins, Tom Mothersdale, Gemma Whelan, Bessie Carter, Sacha Dhawan, Hammed Animashaun and George Fouracres.

	Stevenson, an Olivier and Critics’ Circle award winner, has recently starred in “King and Conqueror” and “Professor T.” Williams’ television credits include “Dune: Prophecy” and “The Crown.” Dhawan currently appears in “Doctor Who” and “The Great,” while Whelan is known for “Game of Thrones” and “The Tower.” Carter stars in Netflix’s “Bridgerton.”

	“An Oak Tree” is directed by Crouch, Karl James and Andy Smith, with music by Pete Gill and piano by Simon Crane.
	

	The production is part of a new Francesca Moody Productions season at The Other Palace that also includes “Garry Starr: Classic Penguins,” running Oct. 22 through Jan. 3, 2027, and “Feeling Afraid As If Something Terrible Is Going To Happen,” running Nov. 19 through Jan. 10, 2027. FMP also produces Hannah Reilly’s “Roleplay,” transferring to Soho Theatre from Oct. 22-Nov. 21, and presents Shedinburgh at the Young Vic’s Maria Studio through Oct. 10.

	Francesca Moody, whose credits include “Fleabag” and “Baby Reindeer,” is the company’s executive producer.

schema.headline: Juliet Stevenson, Olivia Williams Join Tim Crouch’s ‘An Oak Tree’ at the Other Palace (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Banijay to Launch Dating Reality Format ‘Date Knight’ at Mipcom (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Media and entertainment group Banijay Entertainment has unveiled a new dating reality format “Date Knight,” which will join its portfolio of new IP
body:
Media and entertainment group Banijay Entertainment has unveiled a new dating reality format “Date Knight,” which will join its portfolio of new IP heading to TV market Mipcom.

	The show is produced by Nordisk Film TV, part of Banijay Nordic, for Danish public broadcaster DR.

	“Date Knight” invites singles to step into a spectacular “romantasy” world, where epic love and adventure collide. Here, dating becomes roleplay. Reimagined as knights, elves, witches and warriors, the singles first meet and date entirely in character, leaving the rules of modern dating behind. Through grand balls, secret encounters and romantic quests, they will forge connections and take chances on love in ways they might never dare to in real life. 
	

	Born from research illustrating roleplay can boost confidence, empathy and self-awareness, the show explores whether it can become a path to authentic connection. 


	Guided by DR P3 radio host Jannik Schouw and couples therapist and anthropologist Julie Houe, the couples gradually let go of their personas revealing their true selves. But when the costumes come off, will the romance survive beyond the castle walls?

	James Townley, chief content officer, development, Banijay Entertainment, said: “With ‘Date Knight,’ Nordisk Film TV has transformed the powerful cultural trend of romantasy into a highly original dating format. Using roleplay as a gateway to genuine human connection, this visually ambitious, emotionally engaging new series is set to bring a touch of romance to the Croisette.”

	Ulrik Jørgensen, CEO, Nordisk Film TV, added: “’Date Knight’ changes the dynamics of modern dating and introduces a new kind of thoughtful dating. Freeing participants from many of the expectations and insecurities shaping first impressions, the format allows them to be bolder and more emotionally open. The result… humor, surprise and heart-filled connections that transform into compelling love stories.”
	

	Isabella Alonso De Vera Hindkjær, head of DR P3, commented: “We were drawn to ‘Date Knight’ because it offers something genuinely different within the dating genre — an imaginative and entertaining world where contestants can lower their guard, build trust and discover unexpected chemistry. This really is escapist entertainment with real emotional authenticity.”

	The format joins Banijay Entertainment’s Mipcom 2026 slate of original titles, alongside “100 Knives,” “Last One Standing” and “Million Dollar Idea,” as well as upcoming streamer titles “Beat Luke Littler,” “Netflix, Will You Marry Me?,” “Simon Says,” “The Mob” and “Monopoly.”

schema.headline: Banijay to Launch Dating Reality Format ‘Date Knight’ at Mipcom (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Susan Sarandon to Be Honored at Rome Film Festival Sidebar Where ‘The Accompanist’ Will Bow Internationally (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Susan Sarandon will be honored by the Rome Film Festival’s independently run Alice in the City sidebar, which is dedicated to films for children and
body:
Susan Sarandon will be honored by the Rome Film Festival’s independently run Alice in the City sidebar, which is dedicated to films for children and youth.

	Sarandon will be attending the Eternal City fest to promote the international launch of “Silicon Valley” star Zach Woods’ feature film debut “The Accompanist,” in which she stars; and to receive the event’s Womenlands Excellence Award dedicated to outstanding Italian and international women who distinguish themselves in the worlds of culture, entertainment and activism.
	

	In “The Accompanist,” Sarandon plays Sylvia, a chain-smoking, sharp-tongued, first-time foster parent to a spirited eight-year-old named Emily. The indie dramedy launched positively from the Tribeca Film Festival in June.


	“From ‘The Rocky Horror Picture Show’ to ‘The Hunger,’ from ‘The Witches of Eastwick’ to ‘Thelma & Louise,’ to ‘Dead Man Walking,’ Sarandon has spanned decades of cinema, building a gallery of female characters that cannot be reduced to a single model,” the fest said in a statement praising her career. The statement added that the characters she plays in these films are all “Women who question identity, desire, power, rules and freedom.” “But the common thread running through her journey is not only the roles she has chosen,” it continued.

	“It is also her ability to maintain her own autonomy from the Hollywood system, bringing together artistic choices, personal freedom and consistency of her own convictions,” the statement went on to point out.

	Sarandon, who recently attended the Venice Film Festival in September with her latest film, Italian director Andrea Pallaoro’s “The Echo Chamber,” said in Venice that she continues to be shunned by Hollywood over her outspoken support of Palestine.
	

	Previous recipients of Rome’s Alice in the City Womenlands Excellence Award include Paz Vega, Nastassja Kinski and Italy’s Laura Luchetti.

	The Rome Film Festival runs Oct. 13-25.

schema.headline: Susan Sarandon to Be Honored at Rome Film Festival Sidebar Where ‘The Accompanist’ Will Bow Internationally (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Inside the Basque Production Boom: Who Owns the Growth?
description:
The Basque Country has become an increasingly attractive place to make films and television.

	In Bizkaia alone, audiovisual employment rose 50.5% b
body:
The Basque Country has become an increasingly attractive place to make films and television.

	In Bizkaia alone, audiovisual employment rose 50.5% between 2014 and 2024, while the number of companies linked to the sector climbed from 284 to 448. In 2025, the Bilbao Bizkaia Film Commission supported 219 shoots with an estimated economic impact of €138.1 million ($158.45 million).

	The boom has also complicated a simple question: What, exactly, is a Basque production? Is it a project that shoots in the territory, one backed by a Basque company, one made in Euskara, or one whose creative control, intellectual property and long-term economic value remain there?
	

	For Xabi Berzosa of San Sebastian-based Irusoin, the legal answer is relatively simple.


	“From a legal standpoint, if a film is produced by a Basque production company, it’s Basque. That’s simply how it is defined.”

	Then he offers the complication. Irusoin is a co-producer on Nanni Moretti’s latest film “It Will Happen Tonight,” alongside such companies as Fandango and BTeam Prods.

	“The film is Basque, as well as Italian and French,” Berzosa says. “It’s shot in Italy and in the Basque Country, in Italian. … We don’t really feel that’s a portrait of Basque filmmaking nowadays, of course, but legally it’s Basque.”

	For filmmaker Koldo Almandoz, whose Basque-language feature “The Last Goodbye” plays out of competition in San Sebastian’s Official Selection this year, the answer lies somewhere beyond legal definitions. It has to do, he says, with “the soul,” with “the culture, the language, the crews and the intention of the films.”
	

	He is blunter about productions arriving primarily because of tax incentives. “You can call it co-production, but we all know that it’s like they are working as commission agents,” he says. “I don’t consider those Basque productions.”

	Iker Ganuza, president of producers’ association EPE-IBAIA and a producer at Lamia Producciones, approaches the same question from an industrial perspective. “A Basque production is not simply a production filmed in the Basque Country,” he says. For Ganuza, the key questions are where decisions are made, where intellectual property remains, how much Basque talent and business are involved and how much value stays in the region.

	If he had to choose one criterion, it would be “deep-rooted business and creative presence, along with decision-making capacity.”

	That word — deep-rooted — sits uneasily beside an industry that is increasingly mobile. Berzosa puts the principle more simply. “Productions that come for financial reasons will leave for financial reasons.”

	None of the producers argues that attracting international productions is a mistake. “Major international productions have obviously a very positive impact,” Ganuza says. “They create jobs, generate economic activity, and boost international visibility.”

	But, he adds, “once filming wraps up, the intellectual property, business decisions, and much of the future value leave the country.” “Both activities are important, but they are not the same.”

	Berzosa makes a similar distinction between servicing and co-producing. “The obvious solution is to service that shooting,” he says. “You are hired, they come and they go.”

	With Moretti’s film, Irusoin instead became a co-producer, gaining ownership and a deeper involvement in the project. Services, Berzosa says, “help people to work and to have continuity,” but “they don’t develop a local established industry for the long term.”

	Almandoz worries about what happens to that local infrastructure if conditions change.

	“If sometime these fiscal advantages disappear, all these little home companies we had, that were working for us, now absorbed by bigger companies, are they gonna stay, or are they gonna go… to Madrid or Barcelona or Paris?”
	

	He is not predicting collapse. “People are working. There’s an industry. We are growing. We are learning a lot.”But, he adds: “We want to pass from zero to 100 in three years, and I don’t think it’s the way.”

	Language adds another layer. For Berzosa, a film written, shot and released in Euskara is one particularly clear example of a production with cultural weight, but it is not a requirement for something to qualify as Basque. Ganuza likewise argues that the language must be specially protected, while cautioning against making it the sole measure.

	“We can tell Basque stories to the world and also produce universal stories from the Basque Country.” The broader challenge, then, is not simply how to attract more production, but what remains when those productions leave.

	Ganuza says the next phase must focus on making sure international investment strengthens local companies rather than displacing them.

	“The main problem is not a lack of opportunities,” he says. “It is precisely the opposite: there is a huge opportunity, and we must ensure that growth does not leave behind the companies that have built this sector right here.” That may ultimately become a useful measure of success, and one relevant far beyond the Basque Country.

	“We have to start talking about where we want the Basque film industry to be in 2030,” Ganuza says, “not just how many film shoots we’ll have next year.”

schema.headline: Inside the Basque Production Boom: Who Owns the Growth?

title: Parvathy Thiruvothu on Playing a Police Officer in ‘Pradhama Drishtiya Kuttakkar’ and Speaking Out About Misogyny Despite Scrutiny: ‘I Enjoy Watching Patriarchy Fall Apart’
description:
Indian actor Parvathy Thiruvothu has spent two decades fighting the system from outside it – both on screen and off.

	In “Pradhama Drishtiya Kuttak
body:
Indian actor Parvathy Thiruvothu has spent two decades fighting the system from outside it – both on screen and off.

	In “Pradhama Drishtiya Kuttakkar” (“Prima Facie Guilty”), the Shahad Nilambur-directed thriller now running in theaters, she’s finally on the inside, portraying a police officer for the first time in a Malayalam film. But the actor still feels she’s living under constant judgment after speaking out against misogyny in Malayalam cinema nearly a decade ago.
	

	“I loved it,” Thiruvothu says of playing a character embedded inside a state institution for once. “I’ll tell you why, because most of the time people don’t understand what it is like to stay within a rotten structure and try to change it.”


	Thiruvothu, whose credits include “Bangalore Days,” “Take Off,” “Uyare” and “Virus,” has built a two-decade career largely on roles that push against the structures around her characters.

	In “Pradhama Drishtiya Kuttakkar,” produced by Arjun Selva under 11 Icons Film Productions, Thiruvothu plays Aleena Abraham, a woman who becomes a police officer through a compassionate appointment after the death of her husband, also a constable. Set largely inside a local police station, the film follows Aleena alongside fellow officers Divya, Dasan and Sreenath as an unexpected criminal case upends the precinct, testing perceptions of guilt, duty and systemic justice. The film’s plot repeatedly asks how quickly an audience decides someone’s guilt based on incomplete evidence.

	Thiruvothu says the film departs from convention by revealing the central crime within its first 10 to 15 minutes, shifting the tension from whodunit to whether the officers involved will be found out.
	

	The role marks Thiruvothu’s first time in uniform in a Malayalam film, though not her first police role. She played Kranthi Shenoy, a plainclothes deputy commissioner, in the Prime Video series “Dhootha,” and has dubbed the Malayalam-language version of a police officer played by Kareena Kapoor Khan in “Daayra.” Getting the physical details of Aleena right meant training, then deliberately undoing some of it. Thiruvothu learned the correct police salute during preparation, then had to hold something back on camera so the character would not appear well-versed in procedure.She also spent time on set with real policewomen, some of whom worked as extras on their days off, and separately discussed police procedure at length with Indian Police Service officer Ajeetha Begum in the past. 

	Thiruvothu has not watched “Santosh,” Sandhya Suri’s Cannes-debuting film in which Shahana Goswami plays a policewoman who takes up her late husband’s post through a similar compassionate appointment. 

	“I should probably write to Shahana and ask her if there’s a way I can watch it,” Thiruvothu says, noting that “Santosh” was blocked from release in India by the country’s censor board. “That in itself says enough about the movie as to why it’s important.”

	The screenplay for “Pradhama Drishtiya Kuttakkar” was written by P. S. Subramanian and Vijesh Thottungal. Thiruvothu credits Subramanian with the plot’s procedural logic and Thottungal with its emotional core, describing the narration as “two steps forward, one step back,” repeatedly revealing what audiences thought they already understood before raising a new complication.

	Thiruvothu has been the subject of public scrutiny since 2017, when she spoke out about misogyny in the Malayalam film industry, and has since been active with the Women in Cinema Collective and in the aftermath of the Justice Hema Committee report. The committee, formed by the Kerala government in 2017 to investigate sexual harassment and gender discrimination in the Malayalam film industry, submitted its findings in 2019; the report was made public only in August 2024, after a Kerala High Court order, and detailed systemic harassment, wage discrimination and the blacklisting of women who spoke up. 

	“I feel like I’m constantly living that from being in public scrutiny,” Thiruvothu says. “Anything I say or don’t say, there is always a verdict placed on me. And that has been happening since I’d say 2016, since I called out misogyny in cinema. So I feel like most of the time when the cancel train comes, they cancel you, and then they like you again, and then they’ll again cancel you saying that, ‘Oh, you didn’t say anything about this,’ or, ‘You seem to have done that,’ ‘You seem to be on this side.'”
	

	Asked about the state of activism in the Malayalam film industry, Thiruvothu points to the implementation of Internal Complaints Committees on film sets, mandated under India’s sexual harassment law but resisted for years by industry unions, as a concrete gain. “That’s a big win in terms of feeling safe enough at our workplace,” she says, adding that the industry still lags behind Hindi film sets in the number of women working as department heads, cinematographers and editors.

	She also voiced deep skepticism of institutions in India that ask women to simply wait for justice. “Give me this one instance where a woman has been served justice. Give me one instance, and then I will trust,” Thiruvothu says of conversations she has had defending her decision not to pursue legal cases of her own. “The police couldn’t bring up a case where they showed proof that justice was served.”

	She also argues that Malayalam actresses are given far fewer chances to recover from a box-office failure than their male counterparts, even as actors including Mamitha Baiju, Anna Ben and Anaswara Rajan have delivered hits. “The same choice levels or the number of choices that are given to anyone who is male in this industry has to be given to women and other minorities,” she says.

	Thiruvothu is currently working on four projects simultaneously, including “Storm,” a production from Hrithik Roshan’s HRX banner with Prime Video, and the second season of “Dhootha.” She is also attached to two unannounced Hindi projects and to “Homo Sapiens,” an ensemble Malayalam-language film she describes as lighter than her recent work. She says comedy remains the genre she has not been able to break into. 

	“I so want to play rom-coms, comedies,” Thiruvothu says, citing Mike Leigh’s “Happy-Go-Lucky” and Anne Fletcher’s “The Proposal” as reference points. “That is something that no one has even given me a chance to audition. I want to prove that I can do it.”

	Thiruvothu describes her decision to remain in an industry that has, at points, tried to push her out of it as an act of defiance in itself. “My choice to continue to be in the film industry is probably going to always be one of the bravest things that I would do,” she says. “We need a foot soldier who doesn’t give up, and I’m happy to be that foot soldier. And by just existing in this industry, just existing here and refusing to give up, refusing to leave, that in itself is rebellion enough sometimes.”
	

	She says she did not draw the parallel between her own choice and Aleena’s until she watched the finished film. “So for Aleena to say, ‘I’m not running away from this, I’m not going to run away, but I will protect myself and I’ll continue to do my job’ – I felt such a similarity,” Thiruvothu says. “I enjoy watching patriarchy fall apart. I enjoy it, so I would rather stay in.”

schema.headline: Parvathy Thiruvothu on Playing a Police Officer in ‘Pradhama Drishtiya Kuttakkar’ and Speaking Out About Misogyny Despite Scrutiny: ‘I Enjoy Watching Patriarchy Fall Apart’

title: Japan Pitch Heads to Busan Film Festival With Four Co-Production Projects (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Atmovie Inc. will stage Japan Pitch at the 31st Busan International Film Festival, giving four filmmakers from its Atmovie Global Track accelerator
body:
Atmovie Inc. will stage Japan Pitch at the 31st Busan International Film Festival, giving four filmmakers from its Atmovie Global Track accelerator a platform to pitch original feature projects to international buyers and producers.

	Atmovie Global Track, backed by the Japan Creator Support Fund through the Japan Arts Council, was set up to help Japanese film creators break into international co-production deals. As part of the program, the four fellows will present their projects on stage in Busan and hold individual meetings with visiting producers, buyers and festival professionals.
	

	The event runs across two days at the Centum Hotel Emerald Hall. On Oct. 11, Japan Pitch sessions take place and on Oct. 12, one-on-one meetings run, followed by a second round of pitches and a networking reception.


	Kinoshita Yusuke is pitching “Children of the Empire.” Raised in Australia after being born in Tokyo, Kinoshita made his name at Waseda University with the short “Birdcage,” runner-up for the grand prize and audience award at the 2003 Pia Film Festival. His subsequent feature “Water Flower” played the Berlin Film Festival in 2006, and his segment in the anthology “Ten Years Japan,” executive produced by Kore-eda Hirokazu, screened in Busan before releasing theatrically in Japan, Hong Kong and South Korea. “Children of the Empire” was selected for the VIPO Film Lab NY Script Workshop as well as Atmovie Global Track. Kinoshita founded the company Spectra Inc. earlier this year.

	Saito Shiori is developing her first feature documentary, “Omusubi.” Saito spent close to a decade in New York directing and editing documentary and travel programming before co-founding the production company Mimosa LLC in 2021. She is also known for documentary short “Floating in Between.”
	

	Joya Yoshimi is pitching her feature debut, “Almost Goodbye.” Joya worked as a production manager in commercials before relocating to Canada for overseas production work, then returned to Japan in 2020 to resume directing. Her short film credits include “Be Happy Anyway,” “Doughnuts Mori,” “Colors Under the Streetlights,” an official selection in the Vancouver Film Festival’s short film competition, and “Someday.”

	Arai Soji, a Tokyo-based producer and actor, is presenting “Their Own Sake.” Arai has acted in films by Hamaguchi Ryusuke, Guan Hu, Miike Takashi and Danielle Arbid, along with international projects including Canal+’s “Singapura,” Apple TV+’s “Pachinko” and HBO’s “Tokyo Vice.” As a producer, his credits include the Japan-Korea co-produced short “Route 7,” which took home the audience award from the Busan International Short Film Festival and a market pick at Clermont-Ferrand, and the co-production feature “The Penthouse.” His latest project, “Chihiro | Akemi,” landed a spot in the feature competition at the 31st Split Film Festival. Arai previously brought “Their Own Sake” to the 2026 Cannes Film Festival as part of Atmovie Global Track.

	Atmovie Inc. is based in Shibuya, Tokyo, and is led by CEO Moriya Takeshi. The company produces and oversees television dramas, feature films and streaming content.

schema.headline: Japan Pitch Heads to Busan Film Festival With Four Co-Production Projects (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Rima Das, Shan Zuolong, Shim Eun-kyung Named to Busan’s New Currents Jury
description: The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has confirmed Indian director Rima Das, Chinese producer Shan Zuolong and Korean actor Shim Eun-ky
body:
The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has confirmed Indian director Rima Das, Chinese producer Shan Zuolong and Korean actor Shim Eun-kyung as the three jurors for its New Currents Award, a prize that has served as a launchpad for emerging Asian directors.

	Debut feature films screening in BIFF’s Competition or Vision sections are eligible for the award, which comes with a KRW20 million ($14,400) cash prize.


	Das, a filmmaker based in Assam, India, is known for an intimate visual style built around themes of resilience and the human bond with nature. Her films have played at more than 150 festivals and picked up over 75 prizes internationally. Her credits include “Village Rockstars” (2017), “Bulbul Can Sing” (2018), “Tora’s Husband” (2022), “Village Rockstars 2” (2024) and “Not a Hero” (2026), titles that have found berths at festivals including Toronto and Berlin in addition to Busan. “Village Rockstars” took best feature film honors at India’s National Film Awards and went on to become the country’s Academy Awards submission in 2018. “Village Rockstars 2” was honored with the Kim Jiseok Award during BIFF’s 2024 edition, while “Not a Hero” received a Crystal Bear special mention in Berlin’s Generation KPlus section this year. Das belongs to the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and has sat on festival juries before.
	

	Shan’s credits as a producer trace back to “Kaili Blues” (Bi Gan, 2015), which took the best emerging director prize at Locarno, and “Long Day’s Journey Into Night” (Bi Gan, 2018), an Un Certain Regard selection at Cannes. His later slate includes “Love Is a Gun” (Lee Hong-chi, 2023), honored with Venice’s Lion of the Future for best debut feature; “The Botanist” (Jing Yi, 2025), a Grand Prix winner in Berlin’s Generation section; and “Resurrection” (Bi Gan, 2025), which took the Special Prize at Cannes and also received BIFF’s Busan Award for Artistic Contribution when it played in the festival’s inaugural Competition section last year. He joined the Producers Branch of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in 2026.
	

	Shim swept best actress honors at several of Korea’s top ceremonies for “Sunny” (2011) and “Miss Granny” (2014); her “Miss Granny” performance specifically earned wins at the Baeksang Arts Awards and the Chunsa International Film Festival, along with the Buil Film Awards. She went on to build a career in Japan as well, becoming the first Korean actor to claim the Japan Academy Film Prize for best actress, for her role in “The Journalist” (2019). Her latest credit, “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” (2025), took the Golden Leopard at Locarno, a run that also brought her the Kinema Junpo Best Actress Award.

	The 31st BIFF will run Oct. 6-15 at the Busan Cinema Center and other venues throughout the city. The 21st Asian Contents & Film Market will take place Oct. 10-13.

schema.headline: Rima Das, Shan Zuolong, Shim Eun-kyung Named to Busan’s New Currents Jury

title: From Memory to Horror: Eight New Gen Basque Filmmakers to Track
description: For a new generation of Basque filmmakers coming into focus at San Sebastián, stories often begin with something unresolved: an argument a child can
body:
For a new generation of Basque filmmakers coming into focus at San Sebastián, stories often begin with something unresolved: an argument a child cannot remember, the working lives buried in an industrial landscape, a language whose influence reaches beyond the words spoken on screen.

	“My films grow from spending time with people and places, allowing fiction to emerge from those encounters,” Ekain Albite tells Variety. His “Akira” is taking shape between the Basque Country and Georgia. Joana Moya’s upbringing on Bilbao’s industrial Left Bank informs her interest in “who we are beyond work and how the land and its materiality shape us.” For Gemma González Martínez, Basque identity provides a point of departure rather than a limit. “Being Basque gives me a very strong awareness of language, identity, memory and belonging,” she says. “But I don’t see it as a boundary. It is my starting point.”
	

	Across their work, identity, memory and place are testing grounds. “I want cinema to provoke questions rather than provide answers,” says Asier Urbieta. Mikele Landa sees another possibility in that process: “I am tremendously interested in the use of memory as a matter to imagine possible futures, as a tool of resistance.”


	Their routes to a first feature are varied, spanning journalism, cultural production, television, camera crews and years working on other directors’ films. San Sebastián has been part of that trajectory for several: Landa entered Ikusmira Berriak in 2024, Moya followed in 2025 and Albite joins the program this year. With new works from Nitya López and Gemma González Martínez in Zinemira, and Javier Giner entering with buzz in New Directors, the festival offers a meeting point for eight filmmakers with breakout potential.
	
	
		Nitya López	

	After assistant directing-team jobs on “Ane,” “The Good Boss” and “Maixabel,” López makes his feature debut with a problem no amount of production experience can resolve: how to film a memory he doesn’t have. In Zinemira entry “Family Drill” (“Simulacro”), Iraia Elias and Miguel Garcés help him stage the parental confrontation behind a separation that happened when he was four. Rehearsing possible versions of the event raises questions about what he wants from the reconstruction. The Ibarrangelu-born filmmaker’s earlier directing credits include short “Deadly Draw” and “Aloka(h)iru,” an EITB series co-created with Alba Lozano.
	
		Joana Moya	

	Moya’s geology training gives her an unusual qualification for “La Koreana,” a debut feature project in which the mountain has a history of its own. The arrival of Manuela, who comes from Andalusia to a mining settlement in 1960, opens a story that eventually breaks through into 1890. Lazona Zinema and Sirimiri Films, headed by “20,000 Species of Bees” director Estibaliz Urresola,  are producing; last year’s Sideral Award at Ikusmira Berriak brought a €10,000 ($11,600) international distribution minimum guarantee. For the director, whose short “Salt Covers All” reached Hot Docs, the workers’ struggle concerns a still-familiar “search for dignity, time and freedom.”
	
		Mikele Landa	

	Could the grammar of Euskera affect where a filmmaker makes a cut? That is the kind of question occupying Landa as she develops “Senda” with Gariza Films. “I wonder how much one’s mother tongue can shape a director’s particular way to approach filmmaking,” she explained. Her plans include using translation to inform the film’s construction, and casting sessions to continue its research and writing. An EQZE alum with Basque public bradcaster EITB and Berria journalism experience, Landa has taken the project through Noka Mentoring and Ikusmira Berriak. San Sebastián awarded it the Casa Wabi–ESCINE residency prize in 2024.
	
		Ekain Albite	

	Albite’s filmmaking grew out of collaboration at Barcelona film school ESCAC, where he formed Colectivo Negu with Adrià Roca, Nicolau Mallofré and Mikel Ibarguren. After making shorts together, the group directed “Negu Hurbilak,” which received a Special Mention from the Filmmakers of the Present  jury at Locarno in 2023.
	

	He now takes sole directing responsibility with “Akira,” his first feature as a solo director and an Ikusmira Berriak 2026 project. Set between the Basque Country and Georgia, the film centers on a Georgian scrap dealer whose familiar world is unsettled by the arrival of a relative and a journey into the night. “It explores exile and the quiet unraveling of familiar worlds within an endless night,” Albite says. “I’m excited to extend my work beyond one territory and discover how cinema can bring distant lives together.”
	
		Asier Urbieta	

	Who answers for a death when the territory itself changes hands? Urbieta built his 2025 fiction feature debut “Pheasant Island” around that question, bringing Goya Winner Jone Laspiur (“Ane”) and Sambou Diaby into a drama shaped by the Spain-France frontier. It played last year’s San Sebastian as well as Göteborg. “I’m particularly interested in the border, both as a physical and psychological space,” he says. His next film, “Islandia,” will see Urbieta shoot a single continuous take. “It’s an enormous technical challenge, but also a way of putting the characters, the actors and myself at risk — and that interests me greatly,” he told Variety.
	
		Gemma González Martínez	

	Having led Ladyred Producciones since 2010 and founded women’s culture platform KulturFemme, González Martínez brings her documentary feature debut “Daughters of the Sea” (“Las hijas del mar”) to Zinemira. The film finds affinities between Jeju’s women divers and women whose work connects them to the Basque coast.

	“I’m especially excited by projects that allow unexpected international collaborations to emerge,” she says. Already in development are a further “Daughters of the Sea” chapter spanning the Basque Country, Galicia and Brittany, and “Mirror Mirror,” a documentary series examining cultural ecosystems in different countries. Her slate gives that international ambition a concrete next step.
	
		Javier Giner	

	Giner’s journey from Barakaldo to a feature premiere has included film school in Los Angeles, employment at MGM and international relations work at El Deseo, where he also assisted Pedro Almodóvar.

	Following autobiographical series “Yo, adicto,” his debut “This Solitude” (“Esta soledad”) lands in New Directors. Oriol Pla and Marina Salas play a separated couple for whom earning a living and caring for family leave little room to recover their footing. Giner wrote the film with Luisa Matienzo; Filmax has set an Oct. 30 Spanish theatrical release. It brings a long industry apprenticeship, and TV breakout into a new phase.
	
	
		Norma Vila	

	Bilbao-born Norma Vila makes the leap to features with “Carapace” (“Salitre”), a psychological horror film that turns empty-nest anxiety into something disturbing and physical. Starring Nagore Aranburu (“Querer,” “Sundays”) and Haizea Carneros, the film follows a mother whose terror of losing her teenage daughter begins to infect both their home and relationship. Vila came up through camera crews before directing prize-winning fantasy shorts “Jules D.” and “El fin de todas las cosas.” Now her debut lands directly in Sitges’ Official Fantastic Competition before opening San Sebastián’s Horror and Fantasy Film Festival. It marks Vila as a potentially distinctive new Basque genre voice.

title: Clavicular Charged With Rape in Massachusetts, Influencer's Rep Fires Back
description:
Clavicular
                          Charged With Rape, Drugging Woman For Sex
body:
Clavicular
                          Charged With Rape, Drugging Woman For Sex
                          Influencer's Rep Fires Back
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 21, 2026
                            7:33 PM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Clavicular is facing serious charges, including one count of rape, in Massachusetts ... and it appears to be in connection with similar allegations made by a woman who is suing him in civil court.
      
    
            The Bulwark released a report on Monday ... stating Clav has been charged with rape, drugging a person for sex, and providing alcohol to a minor, all related to an alleged incident that went down in May 2025.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            While the alleged victim in the case has not been identified, it appears to be the same incident relayed by influencer Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza in a civil lawsuit she filed earlier this year.
      

            A rep for Clavicular tells TMZ, "She filed a lawsuit and doesn’t include sexual assault as a count. She then amends it and adds it a couple of months later."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The rep said Clav is fighting the civil lawsuit and believes the influencer has evidence to refute her claims.
      
    
            His rep added, "She and her lawyer then go to police."
      
    
            Sources close to Clav believe the entire situation is a shakedown and they "will be fighting this till the end."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As we reported ... Aleksandra alleges Clavicular paid her $1,000 to film videos for him in May 2025 when she was 16 and said he wanted her to be the female face for "looksmaxxing."
      
    
            Mendoza alleged in her civil suit that she met Clav at a house in Cape Cod, Mass., where excessive amounts of alcohol were served, and that she became very intoxicated. She says while she was drunk, Clav had sex with her despite the fact that she was unable to give consent, and then claims she woke up the next morning to him having sex with her again without her consent. The age of legal consent in Massachusetts is 16, so Clavicular is not facing any child sex charges.
      
    
            Clavicular's attorney Steve Kramer told us at the time the civil case was filed ... "We are aware of the complaint recently filed against Mr. Peters [Clavicular]. These are allegations only and remain unproven. Mr. Peters denies the claims and disputes the characterization of events. He will respond through the appropriate legal channels and intends to vigorously defend himself. We will not comment further at this time."

body:
Dolly Parton
                          Flew to Germany for Experimental Cancer Treatment
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 22, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Dolly Parton secretly traveled to Germany for an experimental cancer treatment about a year before her death ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Sources familiar with the situation tell TMZ ... Dolly privately battled cancer during the final year of her life and sought treatment overseas.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We're told the music icon flew to Frankfurt on a private jet to undergo the treatment. It's unclear exactly what the procedure involved ... but our sources say Dolly remained in Germany for about a week before returning home.
      

            We're told Dolly believed the treatment helped restore her strength and felt it had been effective.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Dolly died August 25 following her private battle with cancer. As we first reported, Dolly's death came as a sudden and unexpected shock to those closest to her ... even though people in her inner circle knew she had been sick.
      
    
            Our sources previously told us when loved ones learned Dolly had been hospitalized and wasn't doing well, they began rushing to Nashville to be by her side.
      
    
            Her family held a private ceremony, and she was laid to rest at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in Nashville.
      
    
            The exact type of cancer Dolly battled, and the nature of the experimental treatment, remain unclear.

Carrot Top
                          Vegas Shows On Pause Amid Hospitalization
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Carrot Top's Las Vegas shows at the Luxor have been canceled through next Monday as the comedian remains hospitalized following a suspected overdose involving prescription pills ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            The 61-year-old's performances through Sept. 28 have been called off while he continues receiving medical care.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we first reported Carrot Top, whose real name is Scott Thompson, took prescription pills Friday before suffering the suspected overdose.
      

            We're told the longtime Luxor headliner remains hospitalized but is awake, breathing on his own and continuing to improve.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Police were spotted at his Las Vegas home Friday afternoon ... and it's unclear when he will be back on stage.
